title: From Soup to Nuts
bodyHtml:
Tseltal is a Mayan language spoken by about 590,000 people in the Mexican state of Chiapas. Below are some Tseltal sentences about what people ate, along with their loose English translations. Sg. and pl. are short for singular and plural.

Note: A chicken comb is the crest on top of a chicken's head. A gizzard is an organ that birds use for grinding up food. A tamale is a traditional Mesoamerican dish, made of dough that is steamed in a corn husk or banana leaf. An avocado is a fruit that has a large seed and green flesh with green to purple or black skin. As an avocado ripens, it becomes significantly softer; unlike other fruits, however, it does not become sweet. Panela is a block of unprocessed brown sugar. A tortilla is a thin, circular flatbread usually made from corn rather than wheat, as many other breads are. A radish is a crunchy vegetable with a sharp flavor often used in salads. Marrow is a fatty substance contained in bones, sometimes spread over bread or vegetables. Greens refers to green leafy vegetables that cook down into a mushy mass.

TseltalEnglish
1la jtiʔ te stsalub muteI ate the chicken comb.
2la jweʔ kaxlan wajI ate bread.
3la achik' kaxlan waj ta kajpeYou (sg.) ate bread soaked in coffee.
4la sloʔik chabThey ate honey.
5la atiʔ ʔichYou (sg.) ate chili peppers.
6la ak'ux kajanYou (sg.) ate my corn.
7la jweʔtik jwajtikWe ate our tortillas.
8la sk'ux chenek'She ate beans.
9la sloʔ mankoShe ate a ripe mango.
10la jk'ux te mankoeI ate the unripe mango.
11la sloʔik jloʔbaltikThey ate our bananas.
12la atiʔ te xchaʔ muteYou (sg.) ate the chicken gizzard.
13la ak'ux kalwanextikYou (sg.) ate our radishes.
14la sweʔik te pats'eThey ate the tamales.
15la sk'ux yaskalShe ate her panela chunks.
16la jchik'tik yaʔlel tiʔbalWe ate meat soup.
17la jk'uxtik awajanikWe ate your (pl.) corn.
18la aweʔ te wajeYou (sg.) ate the tortillas.
19la sk'ux bokShe ate raw greens.
20la jtiʔ awichI ate your (sg.) chili peppers.
21la jloʔ te ʔoneI ate the avocados.
22la stiʔik te yoʔtan muteThey ate the chicken heart.
23la sloʔ yonikShe ate their avocados.
24la aloʔ achabYou (sg.) ate your (sg.) honey.
25la stiʔ sejkub wakaxShe ate cow liver.
26la sk'ux sp'olikShe ate their popcorn.

hints.text: Every sentence starts with la, but the word that follows it is not always the same, even though the English always says "ate". Sort the sentences by which "eat" word they use and look at what kind of food each group contains.

Tseltal picks its verb for eating according to the texture or type of the food: soft mushy things, hard crunchy or countable things, breads, and soupy or soaked things each get their own verb. Then, separately, the prefixes and suffixes on the verb mark who ate, and the very same prefixes and suffixes on the noun mark the possessor. A final -e together with te before the noun marks definiteness ("the").

Take sentence 13, la ak'ux kalwanextik = "You (sg.) ate our radishes". The verb carries a- for a 2nd person singular subject; the noun alwanex carries the 1st person prefix k- plus the plural -tik, giving "our". So the person marking on the verb and the possessor marking on the noun use one and the same set of affixes: j-/k- for 1st person, a-/aw- for 2nd, s-/y-/xch- for 3rd, with -tik for 1st person plural and -ik for 2nd/3rd person plural.

explanationHtml:
Step 1: la is the easy part

Every single sentence begins with la, and every English translation is in the past tense. So la just marks a completed action (linguists call this perfective). You cannot work out anything more precise than that from the data, and you do not need to.

Step 2: there is more than one word for "eat"

Look at the second word of each sentence, stripping off the prefix that changes from row to row. You keep meeting the same handful of stems:

  • tiʔ in row 1 (chicken comb), 12 (gizzard), 22 (heart), 25 (liver), 5 and 20 (chili peppers)
  • loʔ in row 4 (honey), 9 (ripe mango), 11 (bananas), 21 and 23 (avocados)
  • k'ux in row 6 and 17 (corn), 8 (beans), 10 (unripe mango), 13 (radishes), 15 (panela chunks), 19 (raw greens), 26 (popcorn)
  • weʔ in row 2 (bread), 7 and 18 (tortillas), 14 (tamales)
  • chik' in row 3 (bread soaked in coffee) and 16 (meat soup)

A pattern jumps out: the verb depends on the kind of food.

  • tiʔ = eat meat and meat-like organs (and, oddly, chili peppers)
  • loʔ = eat soft, mushy things (honey, banana, avocado, a ripe mango)
  • k'ux = eat hard, crunchy or countable things (radish, panela chunks, corn, popcorn, beans, an unripe mango)
  • weʔ = eat breads (bread, tortilla, tamale)
  • chik' = eat soups and things soaked in liquid

Two foods appear twice with two different verbs, and that confirms the rule beautifully: mango is loʔ when ripe (soft) but k'ux when unripe (hard), and greens are k'ux when raw (crunchy) but would take loʔ once cooked into mush.

Step 3: which food breaks the pattern?

Every group above makes sense from the food's texture, with one exception: chili peppers are not meat, yet rows 5 and 20 use tiʔ, the meat verb. That is the odd one out asked for in H1. (In the real language, mushrooms behave the same way.)

Step 4: the prefixes and suffixes

Now compare rows that differ only in who ate:

  • row 1 jtiʔ "I ate", row 5 atiʔ "you (sg.) ate", row 25 stiʔ "she ate", row 22 stiʔik "they ate", row 16 jchik'tik "we ate"

So the subject markers are j- (1st person), a- (2nd), s- (3rd), with -tik for "we" and -ik for plural 2nd/3rd person. The prefixes change shape depending on the following sound: j- becomes k- before a consonant like k'ux (giving jk'ux is written with j, but on nouns you see kajan "my corn"), a- becomes aw- before a vowel (awajanik "your (pl.) corn"), and s- becomes y- before a vowel (yonik "their avocados") and xch- before ch (xchaʔ "its gizzard").

The clever part: the very same affixes mark possession on nouns. Row 6 kajan "my corn", row 24 achab "your honey", row 15 yaskal "her panela chunks", row 26 sp'olik "their popcorn", row 7 jwajtik "our tortillas". Note that a plural suffix on the noun tells you the number of the possessor, not of the thing possessed.

Step 5: "the"

When the English says "the", the noun phrase is wrapped in te ... -e: row 10 te mankoe, row 18 te waje, row 21 te ʔone, row 14 te pats'e. Notice that when the noun already ends in a vowel the extra -e is still written (mankoe). Unpossessed plurals get -etik (kalwanextik shows the possessed form instead).

Step 6: building the answers

Take H3f "She ate cooked greens": cooked greens are mushy, so the verb stem is loʔ; "she" gives s-; the noun bok is bare (no "the", no possessor). Result: la sloʔ bok — exactly the opposite of row 19, where the greens are raw.

Take H3a "We ate the peanuts": peanuts are hard and countable, so k'ux; "we" gives j-...-tik; "the" gives te ... -e around kaxlan chenek'. Result: la jk'uxtik te kaxlan chenek'e.

For H4, marrow is a soft fatty substance, so the meat verb is wrong and the mushy-food verb with a 1st person prefix is right. For H5, toasted tortillas are hard and crunchy rather than soft bread, so the bread verb loses out to the hard-food verb, keeping the 3rd person prefix.

Step 7: kaxlan

Compare row 2 kaxlan waj "bread" with waj "tortilla" (rows 7, 18), and chenek' "beans" with kaxlan chenek' "peanuts". kaxlan marks a foreign or non-indigenous version of a familiar thing (it comes from "Castilian"). So kaxlan ixim, literally "foreign corn", is the grain that Europeans brought: wheat. The proportion also works out neatly: waj is to kaxlan waj (tortilla to bread) as ixim is to kaxlan ixim (corn to wheat).

A note on body parts

In "cow kidney" the official solution writes sk'in wakax, with the 3rd person prefix s- literally giving "cow's kidney" — that is what Tseltal really does, and it matches stsalub mute, sejkub wakax and yoʔtan mute in the data. But the data also allows a solver to conclude there is no prefix there at all, so consistently prefix-free answers were accepted too.
_reviewNotes: Glottal stop transcribed as U+0294 (ʔ) throughout, matching the booklet's IPA-style character; ASCII '?' added as an accepted variant on every affected key. Apostrophes in Tseltal data are typographic right single quotes in the PDF but transcribed as ASCII ' for typability — confirm graders accept both. Points split (H1=2, H2=2, H3 a-g=1 each, H4=1, H5=1, H6=2) is inferred; the official pages show no per-part breakdown. H2/H3b/H3g alternate (prefix-free) answers from the solution's note are included as accepted variants.
